title: Leading at twelve
hook: young Ranjit leads the Sukerchakia misl with his mother-in-law's help

segments.voice: Yesterday, born at Gujranwala: a scarred face, one eye, and a laugh. Your line was one eye, clear vision. Did you manage to laugh at one flaw? Day nine hundred eight.

A council tent. Older men with long service and longer memories sit in a ring, and at the head of it sits a boy. He has the title. His father is gone and the misl is his. What he does not have is years. He doesn't know which chief keeps his word and which one smiles and waits. He has never run a treasury. So the question in the tent isn't who's in charge. It's who's helping the one in charge. Today: leading at twelve.
screen: `A COUNCIL TENT.` → `A BOY AT THE HEAD OF IT.` → `WHO'S HELPING HIM?`

segments.voice: This path has already met the woman at the center of this: Rani Sada Kaur, who led the Kanhaiya misl and whose daughter was married to Ranjit. Today, look at the whole circle around the boy, because the histories don't show a lone genius. They show a team. There was his mother, who held the household and the family's interests in his early years. There were his father's ministers and captains. And there was Sada Kaur, who brought her own riders and her own hard sense to his side. Tradition credits her with steering him through the dangerous early years, and with standing beside him in his first big moves. Here's the turn. Ranjit didn't fight that help. He used it. Some young heirs try to prove they need nobody. Tradition remembers him learning to listen, to watch, and to take advice, until he was ready to stand on his own. And that shape, a leader who receives, is an old one in Sikh memory. When Guru Gobind Singh gave amrit to the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones, tradition says he then asked those five to give it to him. The Guru knelt and received. A later poet hailed him as Guru and disciple both at once. In the Sikh story, being helped is not the opposite of leading. It's part of how leading is done. So the boy at the head of the tent wasn't weak because he needed the people around him. He was a leader because he let them make him one.
screen: `NOT A LONE GENIUS: A TEAM.` · `SADA KAUR AT HIS SIDE.` · `THE GURU KNELT AND RECEIVED.` · `GURU AND DISCIPLE AT ONCE.` · then, large: `HELP MAKES THE LEADER.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the help you've had. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're good at now, or responsible for. Then trace it back: who showed you how? A teacher, an older cousin, a coworker who covered for you, someone who simply believed you could. Let their faces come one at a time. Don't rush. Then think of one place where help is on offer right now and you've been waving it away. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones who gave amrit back to the Guru who knelt to receive it. Leading at twelve, carried by his mother, his father's people and Rani Sada Kaur, the boy learned that being helped is part of leading. Today's word.
Your line: help makes the leader. Today, when someone offers to help, say yes before you say anything else, and then say thank you. Day nine hundred eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Ranjit Singh's early years with Rani Sada Kaur at his side, and remember Guru Gobind Singh asking the Panj Pyare to give him amrit as a picture of a leader who receives.
